text: Here is a strange fact about attention. If you shuffle the words of a sentence, every output vector is the same as before, only shuffled in the same way. Dog bites man and man bites dog hand attention exactly the same collection of vectors, because nothing in the computation says which token came first. Attention sees a bag of words, and a language model needs a sequence, so we have to tell it where each token sits.

The standard solution is surprisingly blunt. For every position in the text there is a position vector, of the same width as the embeddings, and we simply add it to the token's embedding before the first layer. It is like stamping a seat number onto each guest's badge: the badge still says who the guest is, but now it also says where they are sitting. Adding, rather than appending, keeps the width unchanged, and in a space with hundreds of dimensions there is plenty of room for the network to learn to read the two kinds of information apart.

Where do position vectors come from? The simplest answer is to learn them, exactly like token embeddings: a second table with one row for each position up to the longest context the model will see. GPT two does this, with a row for each of its positions. The drawback is that the table has nothing to say about positions beyond its last row, so the model cannot be used on longer texts than it was built for.

The original transformer used a fixed pattern instead, built from sine and cosine waves. Each pair of dimensions holds a wave of a different frequency, from very fast to very slow. Think of the hands of a clock: the second hand moves quickly and the hour hand slowly, and together they give every moment a unique reading. In the same way, the fast waves distinguish neighbouring positions, while the slow waves tell apart positions that are far away.

The waves have a neat property. Moving forward by a fixed number of positions turns each sine and cosine pair by a fixed angle, whatever the starting point, so an offset like three tokens back looks the same everywhere in the sentence, and attention can learn relative positions easily. Many recent models push this idea further with rotary position embeddings, which rotate the queries and keys themselves by an angle that depends on position.

In our own small GPT, we will use the learned version: each token's input is its embedding plus the row of the position table for where it sits. Now every vector carries both what the token is and where it is. All the ingredients are ready, and the next lesson assembles them into the repeating unit of every large language model, the transformer block.
